## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team
does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county,
including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments
drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some
households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune*
investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County:
lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than
expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago,
2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains
**only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is
yours to build.

### A real test

| File | What's in it |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices |
| `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict them; we score you. |

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that
sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your
test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.**

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their
portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate
uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about
*this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE,
and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of
it.

### Rules

::: callout-important
## 1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.

You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than
filtering.

## 2. Stay inside the time window

Open data from 2023–2025 only.

## 3. No leakage

Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for
a house that didn't sell?*

## 4. The outcome stays in dollars

Transform predictors, not `sale_price`.

## 5. No prices from the test fold or the future

No features built from other houses' sale prices.
:::

### Please include in your final rendered qmd for this assignment:

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Model log** | Every model you tried, in order, with CV RMSE and Moran's I. Each row has a note saying why you tried it. |
| **Features** | Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including the spatial ones covered these past few weeks. |
| **Diagnostics** | Residual maps for your baseline and final model, and what changed. |
| **Error analysis** | Where your final model fails worst, and whose homes it over-values (Part 4). |
| **Reasoning** | Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis. |

## Part 0: Setup (provided)

These helpers are to help you get off the ground.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)
library(spdep)
library(nngeo)
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

moran_cv <- function(formula, train, k = 8) {
  model <- lm(formula, data = st_drop_geometry(train))
  residuals <- residuals(model)
  coords <- st_coordinates(
    st_point_on_surface(train)
  )
  neighbors <- spdep::knearneigh(
    coords,
    k = k,
    longlat = FALSE
  )
  neighbors_list <- spdep::knn2nb(neighbors)

  weights <- spdep::nb2listw(
    neighbors_list,
    style = "W",
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  result <- spdep::moran.test(
    residuals,
    weights,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  as.numeric(result$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]])
}

```

### Load both files together (provided)

Build every feature on `all_sales`, so training and test houses get
identical features. Split off `train` again whenever you add something.

```{r}
#| label: load
all_sales <- bind_rows(
  read_csv("chicago_train.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(split = "train"),
  read_csv("chicago_test.csv",  show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(split = "test")
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3435)            # Illinois East State Plane, feet

all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(split)
```

Useful sources: the [Chicago Data
Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org) (find a dataset's ID under its
API button), the Census via `tidycensus`, and Cook County's open data.

## Part 1: Clean and explore

Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and
how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map
of price.

### Clean the data

```{r}
#| label: part-1

#fill na in house features with 0: fireplace = n/a is the same as having 0 fireplaces. This makes the data easier to handle 
all_sales <- all_sales |>
  mutate(
    num_bedrooms = replace_na(num_bedrooms, 0),
    num_full_baths = replace_na(num_full_baths, 0),
    num_half_baths = replace_na(num_half_baths, 0),
    num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces, 0),
    garage_size = replace_na(garage_size, 0),
    central_air = replace_na(central_air, 0),
    one_story = replace_na(one_story, 0),
    full_basement = replace_na(full_basement, 0),
    finished_basement = replace_na(finished_basement, 0),
    brick_stone_ext = replace_na(brick_stone_ext, 0),
    warmairfurnace = replace_na(warmairfurnace, 0)
  )
```

### Rule 1: sales price is equal to or less than 1, likely to be sales that did not go to market

```{r}
# sales price is equal to or less than 1, likely to be sales that did not go to market
all_sales <- all_sales |>
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, format = "%B %d, %Y")
  )
```

### Rule 2: sales date must be between 2023 - 2025: keep within the time frame

```{r}
# sales date must be between 2023 - 2025: keep within the time frame
train_clean <- all_sales |>
  filter(
    split == "train",
    !is.na(sale_price),
    sale_price > 1,
    !is.na(sale_date),
    between(
      sale_date,
      as.Date("2023-01-01"),
      as.Date("2025-12-31")
    )
  )
```

### Finalize data set

```{r}
# Keep test rows
test_clean <- all_sales |>
  filter(split == "test")

# Recombine
all_sales <- bind_rows(train_clean, test_clean)

# Check the number of rows in each split
all_sales |> count(split)

```

**Answer:** What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?

*Your answer:* Building age appears to be strongly associated with price
so we might look at historic district outlines. Both bedroom count and
square footage apprear to be skewed by high outliers. We also can see
that north of 41°N houses the most expensive neighborhoods and south of
that we see the cheapest neighborhoods. This makes us want to inquiry
about the neighborhoods themselves and maybe add in historical redlining
districts.

## Part 2: Build the model

Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can
learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns
`model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`.

### LOADING AND CLEANING ACS DATA

```{r}
# 1. Download ACS 2019–2023 5-year estimates
acs_tracts <- tidycensus::get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    median_age = "B01002_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001",
    median_gross_rent = "B25064_001",
    median_home_value = "B25077_001",
    owner_occupied = "B25003_002",
    renter_occupied = "B25003_003",
    bachelors_or_higher = "B15003_022",
    unemployed = "B23025_005",
    labor_force = "B23025_003",
    vacant = "B25002_003",
    median_realestate_taxes = "B25103_001",
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    valued_millionPLS = "B25075_001",
    work_from_home = "B08301_021"
  ),
  state = "IL",
  county = "Cook",
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    median_income = median_incomeE,
    median_age = median_ageE,
    total_population = total_populationE,
    median_gross_rent = median_gross_rentE,
    median_home_value = median_home_valueE,
    owner_occupied = owner_occupiedE,
    renter_occupied = renter_occupiedE,
    bachelors_or_higher = bachelors_or_higherE,
    vacant = vacantE,
    median_realestate_taxes = median_realestate_taxesE,
    below_poverty = below_povertyE,
    valued_millionPLS = valued_millionPLSE,
    work_from_home = work_from_homeE,
    unemployment_rate = ifelse(
      labor_forceE > 0,
      100 * unemployedE / labor_forceE,
      NA_real_
    ),
    geometry
  ) |>
  sf::st_transform(3435)

# Check ACS download
print(nrow(acs_tracts))


# Define ACS predictor names
acs_vars <- c(
  "median_income",
  "median_age",
  "total_population",
  "median_gross_rent",
  "median_home_value",
  "owner_occupied",
  "renter_occupied",
  "bachelors_or_higher",
  "unemployment_rate",
  "vacant",
  "median_realestate_taxes",
  "below_poverty",
  "valued_millionPLS",
  "work_from_home"
  
)


# 3. Start from sales data and remove old ACS columns
all_sales <- all_sales |>
  select(
    -any_of(acs_vars),
    -matches(
      paste0(
        "^(",
        paste(acs_vars, collapse = "|"),
        ")\\.(x|y)(\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+)?$"
      )
    )
  )


# Join ACS attributes to properties by location
all_sales <- sf::st_join(
  all_sales,
  acs_tracts |>
    select(all_of(acs_vars)),
  join = sf::st_within,
  left = TRUE
)


# Fill missing ACS values using training-set medians
for (v in acs_vars) {

  train_values <- all_sales[[v]][
    all_sales$split == "train" &
      !is.na(all_sales[[v]])
  ]

  # Stop if a variable has no usable training values
  if (length(train_values) == 0) {
    warning(
      paste("No non-missing training values for", v)
    )
    next
  }

  fill_value <- median(train_values, na.rm = TRUE)

  all_sales[[v]][is.na(all_sales[[v]])] <- fill_value
}


print(colSums(is.na(all_sales[, acs_vars])))


train <- all_sales |>
  filter(split == "train")

```

### PARKS DATA LOADING AND CLEANING

```{r}
##PARKS DATA
# Read the parks CSV
parks_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  "data/CPD_Parks_20261019.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = readr::cols(
    the_geom = readr::col_character(),
    .default = readr::col_guess()
  )
)

# Convert the WKT geometry column into an sf object
parks <- sf::st_as_sf(
  parks_raw,
  wkt = "the_geom",
  crs = 4326
)

# Keep useful fields and preserve the geometry
parks <- parks |>
  dplyr::select(
    PARK,
    ACRES,
    geometry = dplyr::all_of(attr(sf::st_geometry(parks), "sf_column"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    park_acres = readr::parse_number(as.character(ACRES))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    park_name = PARK,
    park_acres
  ) |>
  sf::st_transform(3435)

# Transform house locations to the same projected CRS
all_sales <- sf::st_transform(all_sales, 3435)

# Find the nearest park to each house
nearest_park <- sf::st_nearest_feature(
  all_sales,
  parks
)

all_sales$park_distance_m <- as.numeric(
  sf::st_distance(
    all_sales,
    parks[nearest_park, ],
    by_element = TRUE
  )
)

# Find parks within 500 meters of each house (can be changed)
nearby_parks <- sf::st_is_within_distance(
  all_sales,
  parks,
  dist = 500. #TO BE DISCUSSED
)

# Count nearby parks
all_sales$nearby_park_count_500m <- lengths(nearby_parks)

# Sum the acreage of parks within 500 meters
all_sales$nearby_park_acres_500m <- vapply(
  nearby_parks,
  function(i) {
    sum(parks$park_acres[i], na.rm = TRUE)
  },
  numeric(1)
)

summary(
  sf::st_drop_geometry(all_sales)[
    c(
      "park_distance_m",
      "nearby_park_count_500m",
      "nearby_park_acres_500m"
    )
  ]
)

train <- all_sales |>
  filter(split == "train")

```

### SCHOOL PROGRESS REPORTS DATA LOADING AND CLEANING

```{r}
school_locations <- readr::read_csv(
  "data/Chicago_Public_Schools_-_School_Locations_SY2324_20261019.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

school_reports <- readr::read_csv(
  "data/Chicago_Public_Schools_-_School_Progress_Reports_SY2425_20261019.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

school_locations <- school_locations |>
  mutate(School_ID = as.character(School_ID))

school_reports <- school_reports |>
  mutate(School_ID = as.character(School_ID))

# Keep the most recent report for each school
school_reports_latest <- school_reports |>
  filter(!is.na(Progress_Report_Year)) |>
  group_by(School_ID) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = Progress_Report_Year,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Join school reports to school locations (by school ID #)
schools <- school_locations |>
  left_join(
    school_reports_latest |>
      select(
        School_ID,
        Student_Growth_Rating,
        Student_Attainment_Rating,
        Culture_Climate_Rating,
        Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct,
        Graduation_4_Year_School_Pct_Year_2
      ),
    by = "School_ID"
  )

nrow(schools)
names(schools)


#Converting to spatial data
schools <- schools |>
  filter(
    !is.na(Lat),
    !is.na(Long)
  ) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(
    coords = c("Long", "Lat"),
    crs = 4326,
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  sf::st_transform(3435)

all_sales <- sf::st_transform(all_sales, 3435)

#Calculate nearby schools (nearest feature rating)
nearest_school <- sf::st_nearest_feature(
  all_sales,
  schools
)

all_sales$school_distance_m <- as.numeric(
  sf::st_distance(
    all_sales,
    schools[nearest_school, ],
    by_element = TRUE
  )
) * 0.3048

summary(all_sales$school_distance_m)

# Convert unavailable attendance values to NA
schools <- schools |>
  mutate(
    Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct = as.numeric(
      Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct
    ),
    Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct = if_else(
      Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct < 0 |
        Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct > 100,
      NA_real_,
      Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct
    )
  )
nearby_schools <- sf::st_is_within_distance(
  all_sales,
  schools,
  dist = 1600 / 0.3048
)

#Count of shcools within 1600M (CAN BE CHANGED)
all_sales$nearby_school_count_1600m <- lengths(
  nearby_schools
)

all_sales$nearby_school_attendance_1600m <- vapply(
  nearby_schools,
  function(i) {
    values <- schools$Student_Attendance_Avg_Pct[i]

    if (length(values) == 0 || all(is.na(values))) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }

    mean(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  },
  numeric(1)
)

#fill missing values with training data
train_rows <- all_sales$split == "train"

attendance_median <- median(
  all_sales$nearby_school_attendance_1600m[train_rows],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

all_sales$nearby_school_attendance_1600m[
  is.na(all_sales$nearby_school_attendance_1600m)
] <- attendance_median

train <- all_sales |>
  filter(split == "train")
```

```{r}
    stringr::str_detect(
      stringr::str_to_lower(city),
      "chicago"
    ),
    stringr::str_to_upper(state) %in% c("IL", "ILLINOIS")
  )

nrow(chicago_redlining)
table(chicago_redlining$grade, useNA = "ifany")


chicago_redlining <- sf::st_transform(chicago_redlining, 3435)
all_sales <- sf::st_transform(all_sales, 3435)

# which HOLC polygons each house intersects
holc_matches <- sf::st_intersects(all_sales, chicago_redlining)

# Assign the grade 
all_sales$holc_grade <- vapply(
  holc_matches,
  function(i) {
    if (length(i) == 0) {
      return("Outside mapped area")
    }

    grades <- unique(
      na.omit(chicago_redlining$grade[i])
    )

    if (length(grades) == 0) {
      return("Unknown")
    }

    if (length(grades) > 1) {
      return("Multiple grades")
    }

    as.character(grades[1])
  },
  character(1)
)


all_sales$holc_grade <- factor(all_sales$holc_grade)
table(all_sales$holc_grade, useNA = "ifany")

train <- all_sales |>
  filter(split == "train")
```

### MORAN'S I TEST

```{r}
# Calculate Moran's I for model_log
moran_log <- moran_cv(
  formula = f23,
  train = train,
  k = 8
)

moran_log

# Fit the model using the training data
model <- lm(
  formula(f23),
  data = st_drop_geometry(train)
)

# Extract residuals
resid_log <- residuals(model)

# Get coordinates
coords <- st_coordinates(
  st_point_on_surface(train)
)

# Create 8-nearest-neighbor spatial weights
neighbors <- spdep::knearneigh(
  coords,
  k = 8,
  longlat = FALSE
)

neighbors_list <- spdep::knn2nb(neighbors)

weights <- spdep::nb2listw(
  neighbors_list,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Standardize residuals
resid_std <- as.numeric(scale(resid_log))

# Calculate spatially lagged residuals
spatial_lag <- spdep::lag.listw(
  weights,
  resid_std,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Calculate Moran's I
moran_value <- moran_log

# Create plot
moran_df <- data.frame(
  residuals = resid_std,
  spatial_lag = spatial_lag
)

ggplot(moran_df, aes(x = residuals, y = spatial_lag)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Moran Scatterplot: model_log",
    subtitle = paste("Moran's I =", round(moran_value, 4)),
    x = "Standardized Model Residuals",
    y = "Spatially Lagged Residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The Moran's I value is 0.2314 which suggests moderate positive spatial
autocorrelation.

### MAPPING MORAN'S I

```{r}
# Fit model using your updated training data
model <- lm(
  formula(f23),
  data = st_drop_geometry(train)
)

# Add residuals to the spatial data
map_residuals <- train |>
  mutate(residual = residuals(model))

# Map residuals
ggplot(map_residuals) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = residual), size = 0.05) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "purple",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "Residual"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Distribution of House Price Model Residuals",
    subtitle = "Model f23",
    color = "Residual ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The residuals appear to be evenly distributed across our study area and
look visually similar to our initial map of all data points. This
suggests that our residuals are not spatially clustered in any specific
areas of the city and that we have added sufficient predictors to
account for spatial anomalies.

RMSE the most (in order). Median real estate taxes outperformed every
other predictor by a large margin, lowering our RMSE by over 7,000,
making our prediction \$7,000+ closer. The variables from the initial
sale listings - central air, and warm air furnace - made our RMSE worse.
We theorize this is because location and other geospatial factors are
much more influential on sale price than the conditions of the actual
house itself. For example, a small house in a coveted neighborhood will
likely be more expensive than a large house in an undesirable one. This
pattern is true in most cities and across the United States as a whole.

## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays

**4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high
or too low there, and why do you think so?

### Local Moran's I

```{r}
w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(map_residuals_final), k = 5)), style = "W")
lisa_quads <- function(resid, w, alpha = 0.01) {
  lm_perm <- localmoran_perm(resid, w, nsim = 499)
  z   <- resid - mean(resid)
  lag <- lag.listw(w, z)
  p   <- lm_perm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]
  case_when(
    p >= alpha        ~ "Not significant",
    z > 0 & lag > 0   ~ "High-High",
    z < 0 & lag < 0   ~ "Low-Low",
    z > 0 & lag < 0   ~ "High-Low",
    TRUE              ~ "Low-High"
  )
}

map_residuals_final$quad_1 <- lisa_quads(map_residuals_final$residual, w_knn)
table(map_residuals_final$quad_1)
```

```{r}
quad_cols <- c("High-High" = "#b2182b", "Low-Low" = "#2166ac",
               "High-Low" = "#f4a582", "Low-High" = "#92c5de",
               "Not significant" = "grey88")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = filter( map_residuals_final, quad_1 == "Not significant"),
          color = "grey88", size = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(map_residuals_final, quad_1 != "Not significant"),
          aes(color = quad_1), size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = quad_cols) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(color = NULL, title = "Where the errors cluster",
       subtitle = "Red: pockets we under-predict · Blue: pockets we over-predict")
```

*Why the model under-predicts in the red cluster?*

The red cluster is along the North Side lakefront in Lincoln Park and
Lakeview, and here our model guesses too low. We think this is because
our features can measure how far a home is from a park, school or train
station, but not how special that place is. Living near the lake, right
next to Lincoln Park, or inside the Lincoln or Blaine school boundaries
adds a lot to a home’s price, and the model has no way to see that. A
lot of homes here have been fully renovated or rebuilt, but our data
only has the original build year, so the model treats a brand-new
interior like a 120-year-old house.

*Why the model over-predicts in Beverly and the other blue clusters?*

Our model guesses too high in Beverly, and we think it’s because Beverly
looks like a rich North Side neighborhood to our model. The model
doesn't account for how far it is from downtown. It has high incomes,
lots of college graduates, high homeownership and few vacant homes. In
Chicago, most neighborhoods like that are close to the Loop, so when the
model learned that higher income means higher prices, part of that was
really about being central. Beverly is wealthy but about 15 miles from
downtown, so the model gives it a boost it doesn’t earn. Beverly also
has two landmark districts and several Metra stops, and the model
learned those as price boosts mostly from places like Lincoln Park and
Old Town, which are much closer to the downtown. On top of that, a few
very large historic homes on the ridge pull up the neighborhood
averages, so the regular bungalows nearby get predicted higher than they
actually sell for. We see a similar pattern in the blue clusters on the
far Northwest Side, around Edison Park and Norwood Park. These are also
comfortable neighborhoods far from downtown, so the model reads the good
demographics and misses the distance.

**4B.** Assessors judge their work with the **ratio** of predicted value
to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its
owner over-taxed. Does your model's ratio differ by neighborhood income?
Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to "The Tax
Divide."

```{r}
#| label: part-4
ratio_df <- map_residuals_final %>%
  mutate(predicted = sale_price - residual,      # residual = actual - predicted
         ratio     = predicted / sale_price)     # > 1 = over-valued

ratio_df <- ratio_df %>%
  st_join(acs_tracts, join = st_nearest_feature)

ratio_df <- ratio_df %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(median_income.y)) %>%
  mutate(inc_quintile = ntile(median_income.y, 5))   # 1 = poorest ... 5 = richest

ratio_by_income <- ratio_df %>%
  group_by(inc_quintile) %>%
  summarise(n            = n(),
            income_low   = min(median_income.y),
            income_high  = max(median_income.y),
            median_ratio = median(ratio),
            pct_over     = mean(ratio > 1) * 100)

ratio_by_income
```

*Your answers:* Yes, our model’s ratio rises with neighborhood income.
In the poorest fifth of neighborhoods, the typical home is predicted at
89% of its sale price, so it’s under-valued. In the richest fifth, it’s
predicted 13% above its sale price, so it’s over-valued. This is the
opposite of “The Tax Divide,” which found the Assessor over-valued
cheaper homes. We think our model leans on neighborhood features like
median income, which push every home in a rich tract up and every home
in a poor tract down. Our Part 1 cleaning removed no sales, so 108 sales
under \$25,000 that may not be real market sales stayed in. We used the
median ratio so those few extreme sales wouldn’t distort the result.

## Part 5: Predict the test houses (provided)

Refit your final recipe on all training sales, then predict every test
house. Set `f_final` to your final formula.

```{r}
#| label: predict-test
f_final <- ff21
m_final <- lm(f_final, data = st_drop_geometry(train))

test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
check_na(delete.response(terms(f_final)), st_drop_geometry(test))   # check predictors only

preds <- tibble(id = test$id, pred = predict(m_final, st_drop_geometry(test)))

stopifnot(nrow(preds) == nrow(test), all(is.finite(preds$pred)))
write_csv(preds, "team_fun_predictions.csv")

final_cv <- cv_rmse(f_final, train)
final_cv
```

**Final CV RMSE:** $299452.8 When our test RMSE comes back, we'll explain the gap on Q7.

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1.  **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to
    ŷ.

The coefficient of building_000sf (each home's square footage) is
382,377. This means that when holding all other variables constant, an
increase of 1,000 sq feet is associated with a 382,377 higher sale price
based on the training data. Its standard error is 4,961, which tells us
how much the coefficient may vary if we had a different sample.

When the model predicts on the test data, it adds \$382,377 per 1,000 sq
ft (or 382 dollars per 1 sq ft) to every house in every neighborhood. As
we noted earlier, the model applies this average to every house, no
matter the neighborhood. The issue here is that relationships change
across space (spacial non-stationarity), so an additional 500 sq is
worth more in areas with more expensive land. This appears to be one
reason why we get clustered errors.

2.  **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn
    them about?

We would not hand this model to the Assessor yet because our residual
map still shows some spatial clustering. While it is not egregious
(Moran's I is .23 for final model), it does mean that our model is
missing a spatial variable that would more accurately predict the sales
prices. Ultimately, this means that the model could more accurately
predict sales prices. We would warn them that our model underpredicts
the red clustered points in North Side lakefront in Lincoln Park and
Lakeview and that it overpredicts the blue clustered points in Beverly.

We would also tell the assessor that we did relatively light data
manipulation ahead of our regression analysis. We kept all homes in our
data that sold for more than \$1. There were 108 houses that sold for
less than \$25,000. This means that our data presumably included figures
that were non market sales. We chose to prioritize having more data that
could possibly resemble our test data, even if it meant retaining
potential outliers.
